title: Integral Chevalley root model with a prescribed special-fibre pinning
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $S$ be a smooth connected affine finite-type semisimple simply connected $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme]. Here semisimple means that there is no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, solvable means that successive commutator subgroup schemes become trivial, and simply connected means that every surjective homomorphism from a semisimple group with finite central kernel is an isomorphism; finite central means finite-dimensional coordinate algebra and commuting over every commutative $F$-algebra. Fix $T\subseteq B\subseteq S$, $U=R_u(B)$, $(\Phi,\Phi^+,\Delta)$ as in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], and arbitrary simple-root isomorphisms $x_\alpha:\mathbf G_a\xrightarrow{\sim}U_\alpha$ as in [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations]. There exist smooth affine finite-type group schemes $\mathcal G,\mathcal T,\mathcal B,\mathcal U$ over $\mathbf Z$, with closed inclusions $\mathcal T\subseteq\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal G$ and $\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal B$, and root subgroup maps $y_\gamma:\mathbf G_{a,\mathbf Z}\hookrightarrow\mathcal G$ for all $\gamma\in\Phi$, each a homomorphism of group schemes over $\mathbf Z$ which is a closed immersion; the four inclusions are closed immersions and homomorphisms. A group scheme over $\mathbf Z$ here means a scheme over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$ with multiplication, identity and inverse morphisms satisfying the group diagrams, just as in [def-sc-group-scheme]; smooth has the meaning of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. There is an isomorphism $\iota:\mathcal G_F\xrightarrow{\sim}S$ carrying $(\mathcal T_F,\mathcal B_F,\mathcal U_F)$ onto $(T,B,U)$, carrying the image of $(y_\gamma)_F$ onto $U_\gamma$, respecting the labels of roots, and satisfying $\iota\circ(y_\alpha)_F=x_\alpha$ for every $\alpha\in\Delta$. Put $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(\mathcal G_{\mathbf Q})$ and $\mathfrak h=\operatorname{Lie}(\mathcal T_{\mathbf Q})$; here $\operatorname{Lie}(\mathcal G_{\mathbf Q})$ is the space of $\mathbf Q$-linear maps $v:\mathbf Q[\mathcal G_{\mathbf Q}]\to\mathbf Q$ with $v(fg)=\varepsilon(f)v(g)+v(f)\varepsilon(g)$, $\varepsilon$ the evaluation at the identity, with the bracket for which $v\mapsto D_v=(\operatorname{id}\otimes v)\Delta$ carries $[v,w]$ to the commutator $D_vD_w-D_wD_v$ of left-invariant derivations, $\Delta$ the coordinate map of multiplication, and $d(y_\gamma)_{\mathbf Q}(1)$ is the functional $f\mapsto[t^1]\,y_\gamma^*f$. These are a finite-dimensional split semisimple rational Lie algebra and its splitting Cartan subalgebra; the vectors $e_\gamma=d(y_\gamma)_{\mathbf Q}(1)$ together with the simple coroot vectors $h_i$ form a Chevalley basis with the exact root-string and opposite-root normalizations of [lem-sfb-kostant-integral-pbw]. Its based root system is identified with $(\Phi,\Delta)$. Every positive $y_\beta$ factors through $\mathcal U$, and for some enumeration $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_N$ of $\Phi^+$ multiplication gives an isomorphism of $\mathbf Z$-schemes
$$\mathbf A_{\mathbf Z}^{N}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal U,\qquad(t_1,\ldots,t_N)\longmapsto y_{\beta_1}(t_1)\cdots y_{\beta_N}(t_N).$$
It sends the origin to the identity. Empty root systems are allowed, with $\mathcal G=\mathcal T=\mathcal B=\mathcal U=1$ and $\mathfrak g=0$.

source.place: Section 23h, pp.509--511: integral Chevalley construction, equation (153), and the paragraph Reductive groups over Z; Section 23d, Theorem 23.40 and Corollary 23.41, pp.496--497, for matching the prescribed pinning. Ordered integral positive-root coordinates are the integral counterpart of 21.68(a). This statement packages the integral root-model input; the full proof of the integral construction and integral root chart is WANTED in Steinberg, Lectures on Chevalley Groups (1967), not supplied by the field-only Theorem 21.68.

proof.text: Put $X=X^*(T)$ and $V=X\otimes\mathbf Q$. By [lem-sfb-simply-connected-character-lattice], $V$ has basis $\Delta$ and $X$ is the full weight lattice $P$ of $\Phi$. Thus the rational root system in [lem-sfb-root-datum-lattice-embedding] has no central summand. Apply [lem-sfb-chevalley-admissible-representation] to this rational root system, with the prescribed base $\Delta$, obtaining $\mathfrak g_0,\mathfrak h_0,h_\alpha,e_\alpha,\rho,W,\Omega,\Lambda$. In particular $\mathbf Z\Omega=P=X$, $\rho$ is faithful, the lattice is weight-decomposed, and all root divided powers are integral. These are exactly the hypotheses of the integral atlas lemma, not merely integrality of the first root operators.

Form $\mathcal T=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z[P]$, the matrices $y_\gamma(a)=\sum_m\rho(e_\gamma)^m a^m/m!$, and the closure $\mathcal G=\mathcal C$ defined by the kernel $I$ in [lem-sfb-integral-chevalley-weyl-atlas]. Its matrix group operations and integral open atlas are provided by that lemma. Each $y_\gamma$ and $\mathcal T$ factors through the closure: an element of $I$ vanishes on the rational subgroup, so its pullback is zero in the torsion-free rings $\mathbf Z[a]$ and $\mathbf Z[P]$. The identities $y_\gamma(a+b)=y_\gamma(a)y_\gamma(b)$ and $y_\gamma(0)=1$ hold over $\mathbf Q[a,b]$ by the finite exponential formula, hence over $\mathbf Z[a,b]$. In particular all $y_\gamma$ are group homomorphisms over every ring.

source.place: 23h, equation (153), p.510, and Reductive groups over Z, p.511; integral atlas input

proof.text: Each lattice weight summand is a subgroup of the finite free abelian group $\Lambda$, hence finite free by [lem-weil-subgroup-finite-free-abelian-group-free]. Choose bases for these summands. The weight characters define a closed immersion $\mathcal T\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_\Lambda$. Indeed their diagonal matrix entries give $e^\lambda$ for $\lambda\in\Omega$. The inverse diagonal entries are also regular on $\operatorname{GL}_\Lambda$ (entries of the inverse matrix), and give $e^{-\lambda}$. Since $\mathbf Z\Omega=P$, their products give every basis element of $\mathbf Z[P]$, proving surjectivity on coordinate rings. Thus $\mathcal T\hookrightarrow\mathcal G$ is closed as well. A basis of $P$ identifies $\mathbf Z[P]$ with a Laurent polynomial ring over $\mathbf Z$. Each atlas chart is consequently a polynomial Laurent-polynomial scheme, smooth by lifting its variables and units over square-zero ideals. The affine-local smooth-ring characterization in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] now proves that $\mathcal G$ is smooth. It is affine of finite type, being closed in the affine finite-type scheme $\operatorname{GL}_\Lambda$.

source.place: 23h, pp.510-511; explicit character-ring and infinitesimal lifting computations

proof.text: Let $k$ be any algebraically closed field and let $H_k\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(\Lambda\otimes k)$ be the closed group generated by the root matrices. By [lem-sfb-chevalley-root-exponential-group] it is semisimple with maximal torus $D_k(P)$ and the labelled root datum $(P,\Phi,P^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$. All its root matrices and this torus lie in $\mathcal G_k$, so $H_k\subseteq\mathcal G_k$. Conversely every base-changed atlas chart factors through $H_k$: its formula is a product of root matrices, torus elements and the root words $n_w$. The charts cover $\mathcal G_k$, hence the closed ideal of $H_k$ inside $\mathcal G_k$ restricts to zero on an open cover and is zero. Thus $\mathcal G_k=H_k$ as schemes, including the scheme structure. This proves good geometric fibres without assuming that schematic closure commutes with reduction modulo a prime.

source.place: 23.72 and Reductive groups over Z, pp.510-511; atlas comparison

proof.text: Choose an integral cocharacter $q:P\to\mathbf Z$ strictly positive on $\Delta$ and separating the distinct weights of $W$. Such a choice is obtained by a small rational perturbation of a positive functional, avoiding the finitely many weight-equality hyperplanes, then clearing its denominator. Write $p_+(b)=\prod_{\beta\in\Phi^+}y_\beta(b_\beta)$ in increasing-height order and give $b_\beta$ the positive degree $q(\beta)$. The identity $t y_\beta(a)t^{-1}=y_\beta(\beta(t)a)$ follows on each weight block and over $\mathbf Q$, hence integrally coefficient by coefficient. Therefore $p_+^*:\mathbf Z[\operatorname{GL}_\Lambda]\to\mathbf Z[b_\beta]$ is graded for conjugation by $q$. Over every algebraically closed field it is surjective, by [lem-sfb-chevalley-unipotent-polynomial-coordinates].

source.place: 23h, equation (153) and 23.72, pp.510-511; positive-weight grading of the root product

proof.text: For each degree $d$, the target of $p_+^*$ is finite free over $\mathbf Z$, since all variable degrees are strictly positive. Its quotient by the degree-$d$ image is a finitely generated abelian group $C_d$. Graded surjectivity after every algebraically closed field extension gives $C_d\otimes\mathbf Q=0$ and $C_d/pC_d=0$ for every prime $p$ (field extension is injective on vector spaces). The first condition makes $C_d$ finite. If it were nonzero, a maximal proper subgroup would have quotient $\mathbf Z/p$, contradicting the second condition. Thus $C_d=0$ in every degree. This proves integral surjectivity of $p_+^*$, so $p_+$ is a closed immersion. Define $\mathcal U$ to be this closed image; $p_+:\mathbf A^N_{\mathbf Z}\simeq\mathcal U$ is its specified chart.

source.place: Agent coefficient argument for the integral counterpart of 21.68(a); finite graded pieces over Z

proof.text: The field coordinate theorem says that the image of $(p_+)_{\overline{\mathbf Q}}$ is a subgroup. Pull back the defining ideal of $\mathcal U$ along multiplication of two copies of $p_+$, along its inverse, and along any positive $y_\beta$. Each pullback is zero after extending to $\overline{\mathbf Q}$, and hence zero already in $\mathbf Z[b,c]$, $\mathbf Z[b]$ or $\mathbf Z[a]$, all torsion-free. This gives group operations on $\mathcal U$, factors every positive root through it, and puts the identity at $b=0$. It also factors $\mathcal U$ through $\mathcal G$, by the identical argument applied to $I$. The conjugation formula from Step 5 preserves the ordered chart, so $\mathcal T$ normalizes $\mathcal U$ over every ring. These are identities of schemes, with no inference from points over a finite field.

source.place: Agent integral polynomial descent of the subgroup identities from 23h, pp.510-511

proof.text: Order the weight blocks by decreasing $q$. The matrices $p_+(b)$ are block upper unitriangular: this holds over $\mathbf Q$ by [lem-sfb-chevalley-unipotent-polynomial-coordinates], and the zero and identity block entries are integral polynomial identities. Let $\mathcal P$ be the block upper triangular subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}_\Lambda$, defined by the lower-block zero equations, and let $\pi$ be its diagonal-block homomorphism. Each diagonal block is invertible, since their determinant product is a unit. Inside the closed subgroup $\mathcal P_T=\pi^{-1}(\mathcal T)$, the morphism $g\mapsto g\pi(g)^{-1}$ is regular and has values in the block upper unitriangular group. Define $\mathcal B$ by requiring this value to lie in the closed subscheme $\mathcal U$. This is a closed subscheme of $\operatorname{GL}_\Lambda$. The mutually inverse regular maps $(u,t)\mapsto ut$ and $g\mapsto(g\pi(g)^{-1},\pi(g))$ identify it with $\mathcal U\times\mathcal T$.

source.place: Agent block-matrix construction of the integral Borel, following (152)-(153)

proof.text: Since $\mathcal T$ normalizes $\mathcal U$, the multiplication formula $(ut)(u't')=u(tu't^{-1})tt'$ and the analogous inverse formula make $\mathcal B$ a subgroup. It lies in $\mathcal G$, since both factors do. Its sections with $u=1$ and $t=1$ identify $\mathcal T$ and $\mathcal U$ with closed subgroups of $\mathcal B$. Thus all the required inclusions, including their composites into $\mathcal G$, are closed immersions and homomorphisms. The chart rings of $\mathcal U$ and $\mathcal B$ are respectively polynomial and polynomial Laurent-polynomial rings, so the same explicit variable-and-unit lifting as in Step 3 proves smoothness; they are affine of finite type. Finally each positive $y_\beta$ is closed because its product-chart coordinates are $b_\beta=a$ and all other $b_\gamma=0$. For a negative root use the same construction with $-\Delta$ in place of $\Delta$, obtaining a closed negative-root product image in $\operatorname{GL}_\Lambda$ and the same coordinate-axis argument. Factoring these closed maps through the closed subgroup $\mathcal G$ preserves their surjective coordinate maps.

source.place: Agent verification of the integral group and subgroup structures and root immersions

proof.text: Over $F$, Step 4 identifies $\mathcal G_F$ with the semisimple group of the full-weight representation. The root matrices are closed additive subgroups with nonzero tangent characters $\gamma$, by [lem-sfb-chevalley-exponential-big-cell], and hence are exactly the labelled root subgroups by [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations]. Apply [lem-sfb-regular-cocharacter-borel-description] to the cocharacter $q$ of Step 5 to obtain the Borel for $\Phi^+$. Its unipotent radical is the ordered product of these positive root subgroups by [lem-sfb-borel-root-product-coordinates]; therefore it is precisely $\mathcal U_F$. Its Borel is $\mathcal U_F\mathcal T_F=\mathcal B_F$ by [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure].

The based root data of $(\mathcal G_F,\mathcal T_F)$ and $(S,T)$ agree: both have character lattice $P=X$ and the given roots and coroots. Apply [lem-sfb-root-datum-isogeny-realization] with $u=\operatorname{id}_P$, the identity root bijection and every $q_\alpha=1$. Its isomorphism criterion gives an isomorphism $g:\mathcal G_F\simeq S$ inducing this labelled torus identification. Uniqueness of the root subgroup for a torus character gives $g((y_\gamma)_F(\mathbf G_a))=U_\gamma$ for every root. Since an automorphism of the scheme $\mathbf A^1_F$ has polynomial degree one (multiply degrees with its polynomial inverse), and a group homomorphism fixes zero, write $g\circ(y_\alpha)_F=x_\alpha\circ(a\mapsto c_\alpha a)$ with $c_\alpha\in F^\times$ for $\alpha\in\Delta$.

source.place: 23.9 and 23.5; explicit unpinned isomorphism before the 23.39 adjustment

proof.text: Choose $d>0$ with $dP\subseteq\mathbf Z\Delta$, by expressing a basis of $P$ rationally in the basis $\Delta$ and clearing denominators. For every simple root choose $z_\alpha\in F^\times$ with $z_\alpha^d=c_\alpha^{-1}$, using algebraic closedness. Define $f:\mathbf Z\Delta\to F^\times$ by $f(\alpha)=z_\alpha$ and $\tau:P\to F^\times$ by $\tau(\lambda)=f(d\lambda)$. Then $\tau(\alpha)=c_\alpha^{-1}$. The character antiduality [lem-sfb-multiplicative-character-antiduality] identifies $T$ with $D_F(P)$, so $\tau$ is a point $t\in T(F)$. Set $\iota=\operatorname{Int}(t)\circ g$. The root-conjugation formula gives $\iota\circ(y_\alpha)_F(a)=x_\alpha(\alpha(t)c_\alpha a)=x_\alpha(a)$. It preserves every labelled root subgroup and $T$. Positive-root products and $B=U\rtimes T$ show that it sends $(\mathcal B_F,\mathcal U_F)$ to $(B,U)$. This adjustment uses no inverse to $d$ in $F$, so also works when the characteristic divides $d$.

source.place: 23.39-23.41, pp.496-497; explicit extension of simple-root scalars to the torus

proof.text: The open identity chart identifies the local rings at the identity, hence their derivation spaces. Differentiate the integral identity chart $\theta_1$ at $(0,1,0)$ over $\mathbf Q$. It identifies $\operatorname{Lie}(\mathcal G_{\mathbf Q})$, inside $\operatorname{End}(W)$, with the direct sum of $\operatorname{Lie}(\mathcal T_{\mathbf Q})$ and the lines $\mathbf Q\rho(e_\gamma)$. The coefficient of $a$ in $y_\gamma(a)$ is $\rho(e_\gamma)$. For $h\in\mathfrak h_0$, the diagonal matrix $\rho(h)$ has entries $\lambda(h)$ on $W_\lambda$; hence it is exactly the torus tangent functional $e^\lambda\mapsto\lambda(h)$. Since $P$ spans $\mathfrak h_0^\vee$, this identifies $\mathfrak h_0$ with the torus Lie algebra. Thus the faithful representation $\rho$ identifies all of $\mathfrak g_0$ with $\operatorname{Lie}(\mathcal G_{\mathbf Q})$. In the matrix coordinates $X_{ij}$, a left-invariant derivation associated to a tangent matrix $A$ satisfies $D_A(X)=XA$; consequently $(D_AD_B-D_BD_A)(X)=X(AB-BA)$. The bracket specified in the item is therefore the usual matrix commutator, so this is a Lie algebra isomorphism.

source.place: 23h, Chevalley basis and (153), pp.508-510; derivative of the integral identity chart

proof.text: Under this Lie algebra isomorphism, $d(y_\gamma)_{\mathbf Q}(1)$ is $e_\gamma$ and the simple torus coroot tangent vectors are $h_i$: the coroot on a weight summand is $s\mapsto s^{c_{\alpha_i}(\lambda)}$, whose coefficient at $s=1$ is $c_{\alpha_i}(\lambda)$. The Chevalley-basis identities supplied by [lem-sfb-chevalley-admissible-representation] are exactly the root-string and opposite-root identities in the statement of [lem-sfb-kostant-integral-pbw]. This proves the required split semisimple rational Lie algebra, Cartan, labels and normalizations. The positive chart is the integral isomorphism constructed in Steps 5-7, and sends zero to the identity. If $\Phi$ is empty, Step 1 gives $P=0$, the atlas closure and all the constructed subgroups are $1$, and $\mathfrak g_0=0$. Step 11 still gives $1\simeq S$, so this case satisfies every clause too.

source.place: 23h, pp.508-511; comparison with the exact Kostant PBW basis conventions
